analysis.one_liner: Taxes fossil fuel carbon emissions and returns the money through payroll tax cuts and benefit payments.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan $30-per-ton carbon tax bill that returned revenue through payroll cuts and Social Security bonuses never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SWAP Act would put a $30-per-ton tax on carbon dioxide from coal, oil, and natural gas, rising about 5% a year, with extra increases if emissions targets are missed. Roughly 70% of the money would cut payroll taxes, 10% would go out as equal bonus payments to Social Security beneficiaries, and 20% would fund a trust fund for low-income energy bill relief, climate adaptation, and clean energy research. In exchange, the bill would bar the EPA from writing new greenhouse gas regulations for about 12 years, with carve-outs for car, truck, aircraft, and some methane rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers would see a cut in the Social Security payroll tax, funded by the carbon tax, with the Treasury making the Social Security trust funds whole. Every Social Security and railroad retirement beneficiary would get an equal annual bonus payment. Low-income households would get state block grants to offset higher energy bills, and the country would get a rising, enforceable price on carbon emissions. Cleaner energy sources would gain a price advantage over fossil fuels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, Social Security recipients, low-income households

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2021 it would cut the employee and self-employment Social Security payroll tax rate by a 'reduced carbon rate' (at least 1 percentage point in 2021, rising with carbon tax receipts), with the Treasury transferring general funds to the Social Security trust funds so benefits are untouched.

It would pay an equal annual bonus to every Social Security and railroad retirement beneficiary, funded by 7.5% of carbon tax receipts (the CRS summary describes 10% of revenue going to additional beneficiary payments).

Half of a new Carbon Trust Fund (about 10% of total revenue) would go to state block grants offsetting higher energy costs for low-income households; the other half to climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, energy efficiency, and research programs.

It would tax carbon at $30 per metric ton starting in 2021, rising 5% plus inflation each year, with an automatic extra $3-per-ton increase every two years if actual emissions exceed the schedule in the bill, and a 3x penalty for nonpayment.
To protect energy-intensive manufacturers, it would rebates the carbon tax on exports and levy an equivalent border tax on covered imports from countries without comparable carbon pricing.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and importers pay the tax at the mine mouth, refinery, or gas processing plant, and energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, chemicals, aluminum and more) pay it on industrial process emissions; much of that cost would be passed through to consumers in higher fuel and electricity prices. The EPA would also give up its authority to write new greenhouse gas regulations for roughly 12 years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive manufacturers

drawbacks.text: In exchange for the tax, the bill would ban the EPA from publishing or enforcing any rule limiting greenhouse gas emissions on the basis of their climate effects for about 12 years (until 2034), only lifting the ban early if emissions exceed the bill's targets — locking in the carbon tax as the country's only federal climate tool for that period, while car, truck, nonroad, aircraft, and certain oil-and-gas methane rules are preserved as exceptions.

Households would pay the tax through higher fuel and electricity prices, and only about 10% of revenue would go directly to offsetting low-income energy bills; the payroll tax cut returns money in proportion to wages, so higher earners recoup more in dollars, and people with no paycheck and no Social Security benefit would bear higher prices with no offset.

Starting at $30 per ton, the tax is well below what most economists estimate is needed to match the damages from a ton of carbon, which is precisely why the bill pairs it with automatic escalators — and why critics of the regulatory moratorium argue the trade gives up too much for too little.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine climate policy with an unusually worker-friendly revenue design: a rising carbon price with most of the money returned through payroll cuts, equal payments to retirees, and low-income energy relief, plus border adjustments to protect manufacturers. The serious cost is the trade at its center — a 12-year ban on EPA greenhouse gas regulation that takes the stricter regulatory tool off the table even if the tax proves too weak, and the revenue recycling leaves out anyone without wages or benefits. Climate advocates would fairly call the moratorium a bad bargain; opponents of carbon pricing would call the tax itself the problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees, none of which ever scheduled a markup or vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Francis Rooney, a Republican from Florida, introduced the bill on July 25, 2019 with Rep. Dan Lipinski, a Democrat from Illinois, as the only other sponsor.

The House referred it the same day to three committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Science, Space, and Technology — and a few days later to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No committee ever reported the bill, no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the congressional record shows no further action of any kind before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they never faced the $30-per-ton tax and its 3x penalty, and the EPA's regulatory authority stayed exactly as it was rather than being traded away in a 12-year moratorium.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided a carbon tax

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SWAP Act, a carbon tax with payroll tax cuts and a 12-year EPA regulatory moratorium.

for.name: Rep. Dan Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Joined Rooney in introducing the bill, making it one of the few carbon tax proposals with a Democratic cosponsor that Congress.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill's core tax provisions on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the record shows no action after the referral.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which shared jurisdiction over the EPA moratorium provisions, referred the bill to a subcommittee and took no further action on it.

against.name: Fossil fuel and energy-intensive industries
against.what_they_did: Opposed carbon tax legislation as a general matter during this period, though no formal opposition to this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members were attached to the bill — one Republican and one Democrat — and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no partisan split either way.

industries.note: The bill taxes coal at the mine mouth — roughly $30 per ton of carbon dioxide, which works out to about $60 or more per ton of coal — with triple penalties for nonpayment. In return, the 12-year EPA moratorium would shield coal-fired generation from new federal greenhouse gas rules, locking in the tax as the only constraint.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Refineries and gas processing plants would pay the tax at their exit points, though carbon captured for enhanced oil recovery would qualify for refunds. The moratorium would block most new EPA climate rules on combusted fuels, while preserving existing methane standards for oil and gas facilities.

Power plants would escape new EPA greenhouse gas regulation for 12 years while the carbon tax was collected on their fuel, passing costs to ratepayers. The bill would make the tax the sole federal climate lever for electricity, entrenching fossil generation's regulatory position even as it taxed it.

These industries would pay the tax on listed industrial process emissions, but the bill's border adjustments would rebate the tax on their exports and levy equivalent charges on competing imports, largely insulating them from losing ground to foreign producers.

A rising price on coal, oil, and gas would make wind, solar, and efficiency more cost-competitive, and the Carbon Trust Fund would direct money to sequestration, energy efficiency, and advanced research programs.
